Sensitivity analyses

The constrained variants of the GRU and the LSTM shifted individual values, lowering the cohort separation of the entropy by 0.03 to 0.05 and raising that of the density by 0.02 overall, but changed no ordering: the entropy remained below chance, the density at most weakly above it, and at the patient level the density stayed below the entropy in every variant (Supplementary Table 6). Among the further density definitions, a shared covariance, a per-class Gaussian mixture, and the class-conditional Gaussian were above 0.5 in all seven configurations and the relative Mahalanobis distance of Ren et al. 26 in five of seven, all below 0.57; a backgroundcorrected relative density score was above 0.5 in two and a density on length-normalized representations in two (Supplementary Table 6, Supplementary Fig. 2).

Restricting the external cohort to the 56,556 stays that satisfy the MIMIC-IV admission criterion changed every uncertainty measure by less than 0.01 (Supplementary Table 2), and refitting the density on a class-balanced training subset changed its cohort separation by less than 0.01 (Supplementary Note 7). At a classification threshold of 0.5, every uncertainty measure identified errors less well. The Monte Carlo entropy and the single-model entropy stayed within 0.01 of each other at both thresholds (0.761 vs 0.755, 0.753 vs 0.744, and 0.770 vs 0.767 at 0.5), and the density on length-normalized representations exceeded the singlemodel entropy for the GRU (0.764 vs 0.755; Supplementary Table 8, Supplementary Note 2).

Finally, 66 of the 70 trained models had reached their lowest validation loss before the final epoch of the fixed training length, and assessing each base model at that epoch instead of the end of training changed no conclusion (Supplementary Note 10; Supplementary Table 10; Supplementary Table 11).

Discussion

After transfer to another hospital system, discrimination and calibration declined, but no uncertainty measure rose to signal this loss: predictive entropy and mutual information were in fact lower in the external cohort. Within the external cohort uncertainty however identified the single predictions most likely to be wrong, and deferring the most uncertain patients removed most misclassifications, mostly false alarms, from the predictions that remained. The uncertainty measure that served best on both patient-level questions was the simplest one, the predictive entropy of the model itself; sampling-based and distance-based uncertainty measures added little or did worse. Uncertainty, as measured by predictive entropy, thus ranked predictions by their reliability but did not reveal that the model as a whole had become less reliable.

Most external patients received a low predicted risk of death (Supplementary Fig. 1); predictions near 0% or 100% have low entropy, whereas predictions near 50% have high entropy because survival and death are considered equally likely. Low entropy therefore indicates a more certain prediction, not a correct one: it decreased even though the models became less able to distinguish survivors from non-survivors and produced overly extreme risk estimates (calibration slopes below 1). Ovadia et al. 7 showed that good calibration on the original data does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimates when the data change; transfer between hospital systems is a clinical instance of this. Monitoring for an increase in entropy would have failed to flag the observed deterioration.

Disagreement between repeated predictions did not indicate the deterioration either; two properties of mutual information may explain why. It accounted for only a few percent of the total predictive uncertainty, and for the GRU and the transformer the difference between cohorts largely disappeared when patients were compared within deciles of predicted risk (Supplementary Note 9), so that it partly reflected the distribution of predicted risks. In addition, ensemble members and dropout passes may have made similar errors after transfer; agreement among repeated predictions does not imply that they are correct.

These results follow from what the measures estimate: entropy and mutual information describe the predicted outcome and can therefore rank errors but need not rise when the inputs change, whereas representation density describes the inputs and can register a change in the population but says nothing about whether a given prediction is correct. That the density separated the cohorts only weakly leaves two explanations: the two cohorts look alike in the learned representation, or the representation or the density estimator overlooked the changes that mattered for prediction. The outcome is in line with Postels et al. 27 , who found that strong detection of unfamiliar inputs by deterministic methods does not guarantee reliable uncertainty under continuous distribution shift, and contrasts with the image-benchmark results of Mukhoti et al. 28 , where such densities matched deep ensembles.

Predictive entropy still helped identify patient-level errors within the external cohort. Most correctly classified patients had very low predicted risks and low entropy. Misclassified patients often had intermediate predicted risks, where entropy is higher. When a fixed proportion of predictions is selected for review, what matters is whether incorrect predictions rank above correct ones. Entropy can therefore help select individual predictions for review even when its overall level is lower in the external cohort. Compared with the internal test set, error detection by entropy lost 0.007 to 0.020 in AUROC and the excess area rose by about a third. After transfer, entropy still separated incorrect from correct predictions almost as well as at the development site, but it gave no indication that the model had moved to a hospital system where it performed worse.

Our main Gaussian density score identified errors best in the GRU, where it ranked patients most similarly to entropy. The density based on length-normalized representations also followed entropy closely and performed best among the density measures (Supplementary Table 7).

High logit variance, which measures variation in the model's internal scores across dropout passes, tended to prioritize correct predictions for review (Supplementary Note 9). High values often occurred at very low or very high predicted risks, where most classifications were correct. At these extremes, substantial differences in internal scores can translate into only small differences in predicted probabilities. This may partly explain why logit variance was a poor indicator of prediction errors.

The most actionable finding is that predictive entropy ranked errors within the external cohort and supported selective deferral: it requires no additional training or repeated passes, can be reported with every prediction 13 , and reviewing one in five patients would have reached about 70% of all misclassifications (Fig. 5; Supplementary Fig. 8). A prespecified entropy threshold, informed by the entropy on the internal test cohort, could trigger review of the patient record, missing measurements, and model output before the prediction informs care. Whether entropy ranks errors in a new setting, and at which threshold, can itself only be verified once outcomes are known, as for calibration; in our transfer this property carried over with modest loss (Supplementary Table 12), but that is not guaranteed elsewhere.

Such a workflow could contribute to human oversight of high-risk AI systems under Article 14 of the EU AI Act 16 . The threshold should be chosen against an acceptable residual error rate and available review capacity and the rule must state which errors it targets: because entropy is highest at a predicted risk of 50% and low near 0%, the rule evaluated here selected almost exclusively false alarms, while most remaining errors were deaths among patients classified as low risk (Supplementary Table 9; Supplementary Fig. 8). Such unflagged errors could create false reassurance, and low entropy should not waive critical review, especially when other clinical concerns are present. How such information is presented matters: limited AI literacy has been identified as a barrier to using model transparency information for oversight 29 , which makes AI competencies an essential part of medical training 30 . Post-market monitoring should not rely solely on the model's own uncertainty. Article 72 of the EU AI Act and Article 83 of the Medical Device Regulation require ongoing monitoring of high-risk AI systems and medical devices, respectively 16, 17 . Finlayson et al. 31 described how changes in patient populations, clinical practice, and data recording can undermine clinical AI systems. Our findings add that poorer performance need not be accompanied by increases in entropy or mutual information, but predictive entropy is a valuable uncertainty measure before true outcomes are known.

Monitoring should include regular checks of patient characteristics, missing measurements, and data recording practices, which can begin before outcomes are known. Once outcomes become available, planned audits should assess how well the model still separates patients with and without the outcome of the event that the model predicts, how closely predicted risks match observed outcomes across the risk range, and how often clinically important errors occur. These audits should specifically examine deaths among patients classified as low risk and check whether the review rule still selects the errors it was designed to identify. Shared terminologies and standards-based repositories such as openEHR support data interoperability across institutions 32 . However, harmonized data structures do not ensure model generalizability, making local validation and ongoing monitoring essential.

Although representation density separated the cohorts only weakly, tracking its distribution across many patients might help identify changes that warrant investigation. Whether this provides a timely and reliable monitoring measure, including for changes within individual hospitals 33 , remains to be tested. As the models themselves gave no such clue, information on the model's development population may help clinicians assess whether it is being applied to patients and clinical settings similar to those in which it was developed 34.

This study has three main limitations. First, its scope: it examined a single prediction task, inhospital mortality from the first 48 hours, a single transfer between two US critical care databases, and 13 routinely charted variables, with glucose and pH as the only laboratory values and no medications. The evaluation framework applies to other settings, but whether the findings, including the deferral results, hold for other outcomes, health systems, and richer inputs remains to be tested.

Second, the comparison of uncertainty methods is bounded in two ways. Other distance-aware approaches, such as spectral-normalized Gaussian processes 35 and deterministic uncertainty quantification 36 , were not evaluated, and the encoder constraints bound distances only across the final layer, not end to end.

Third, the design is retrospective and the statistics describe model variability, not patient sampling. Intervals reflect variability across training runs on fixed cohorts; differences between the hospitals within eICU-CRD were not analyzed, and the breakdown of deferred errors was conducted after the main results were known. Selective prediction was evaluated by deferring the most uncertain patients and measuring errors among the remaining ones; the consequences of false alarms and missed deaths were not weighed against each other, and how such deferral would affect clinical decisions in prospective use was not assessed.

After transfer between hospital systems, model discrimination and calibration worsened while predictive entropy decreased. Representation density only weakly distinguished patients from the two cohorts, whereas predictive entropy was more useful for identifying errors and selecting predictions for review within the external cohort. These findings highlight the distinction between detecting changes in the patient population and identifying individual prediction errors. A model whose performance has worsened may nevertheless appear more confident.

Predictive entropy could help prioritize clinical review, but lower error rates among predictions not selected for review do not establish that review improves clinical decisions. Under the review rule evaluated here, most remaining errors involved patients who died despite being classified as low risk. Clinical use therefore requires validation in the receiving hospital and prospective evaluation of review thresholds and workflows, including which errors remain undetected and how much clinician time review requires. Model performance should continue to be monitored after deployment as patient outcomes become available.

Methods

Study design and data sources

In this retrospective study we developed in-hospital mortality prediction models with MIMIC-IV v3.1 as the development database and eICU-CRD v2.0 as an external transfer cohort 37, 38 . Both are de-identified critical care databases from hospitals in the United States and are available through PhysioNet under credentialed access. Both cohorts were restricted to adults, ICU stays of at least 48 hours, and hospital admissions with a single ICU stay; a patient with several hospital admissions contributes each of them. MIMIC-IV patients were split at random, with 20% held out as the internal test set so that no patient contributes to both sets; the remaining 80% formed the training pool, part of which served as the validation split for hyperparameter selection. All included eICU-CRD stays were used for evaluation only.

Outcome and predictors

The outcome was in-hospital mortality, predicted from the first 48 hours of the ICU stay, following the benchmark task of Harutyunyan et al 39 . Thirteen routinely charted variables were extracted for each of the 48 hours (Supplementary Table 1). Multiple measurements within one hour were averaged, as in MIMIC-Extract 40 rather than represented by the last measurement as in the logic of Harutyunyan et al. Missing hours were filled with the last available value of the same patient, hours before the first measurement with the first observed value, and variables never measured with a clinical default 41 . Continuous variables were standardized with the mean and standard deviation of the MIMIC-IV training data, and the same values were applied to eICU-CRD; standardizing the external cohort with its own statistics would have removed part of the shift the study is designed to measure. The in-hospital mortality rate of the training pool was 12.88% (Table 1).

Model development

We compared three base model architectures that are widely used for clinical time series 42, 43 ; a long short-term memory network (LSTM), which is a baseline of mortality benchmarks 39, 44 , a gated recurrent unit (GRU), the second widely used recurrent variant for irregularly sampled clinical time series 45 and a transformer encoder 46 , which relates all hours of a stay to each other instead of reading them in sequence. Each architecture condenses the 48 hours into an internal representation of the patient, from which a final layer computes the predicted probability.

One of the uncertainty measures, the representation density, scores a patient by how close the patient's internal representation lies to those of the training cohort. This assumes that patients who differ in their inputs also differ in the model's representations 36 . To explore whether enforcing this property has an impact on the results, we trained additional variants of the GRU and LSTM in which spectral normalization limits how strongly the network can stretch differences between patients in the representation space, and a residual block limits how strongly it can compress them 28, 35, 47 . The residual block is the last layer before the prediction head and bounds distances only across this layer, not across the recurrent layers before it (Supplementary Note 3).

Models were trained with the Adam optimizer 48 and binary cross-entropy. Hyperparameters, including the number of passes through the training data (epochs, 10 to 40), were selected per architecture with Optuna 49 via a validation split of the training pool (Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Note 4); the constrained variants used those of their base architecture. Each model was trained ten times with different random seeds, and the ten models of an architecture were also combined into a deep ensemble by averaging their predicted probabilities 50 . Through Monte Carlo dropout, we obtain a predictive distribution for each patient using 30 dropout masks 51 . The passes used the trained deterministic models themselves, with every dropout layer that was active in training also active at prediction time. The dropout uncertainty measures were calculated from the 30 predicted mortality probabilities and their corresponding log-odds. The equations for all components are given in Supplementary Note 1.

Each model returns an estimated probability that the patient dies in hospital. A prediction was classified as positive if this probability exceeded 0.1288, the mortality rate of the training pool. A prediction was therefore misclassified if the classification differed from the observed outcome. A threshold of 0.5 was examined as a sensitivity analysis in Supplementary Note 2.

Uncertainty measures

We compared three uncertainty measures, all computed per patient.

The first is the predictive entropy of a single model. It is highest when the predicted probability is near 0.5 and zero when the model is certain:

The second comes from repeating a prediction either through T=30 Monte Carlo dropout passes or through the T=10 members of a deep ensemble. With 𝑝 𝑖 (𝑡) being the prediction of pass or member 𝑡, the entropy of the averaged prediction is split into a part that the repeated predictions share and a part that reflects their disagreement 51, 52 : 𝑈 alea (𝑖)= 1 𝑇 ∑ 𝐻 𝑇 𝑡=1 (𝑝 𝑖 (𝑡) ).

(3) MI(𝑖)=𝑈 total (𝑖)-𝑈 alea (𝑖)≥0.

Total predictive uncertainty (𝑈 total ) is the entropy of the averaged mortality prediction. The aleatoric component (𝑈 alea ) is the average entropy of the individual predictions and represents uncertainty within those predictions. Their difference, mutual information (MI), measures disagreement between predictions and serves as the epistemic uncertainty measure. MI is zero when all predictions agree, even if each prediction remains uncertain. These definitions apply to both Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles. For Monte Carlo dropout, we also calculated the logit variance, the variance of the log-odds across the 30 passes, as a second measure of epistemic uncertainty (Supplementary Note 1, Eq. S7).

The third kind, representation density, is computed from a single forward pass of a single model. Following deep deterministic uncertainty 28 , a Gaussian model with one component per outcome class is fitted to the internal representations ℎ of the training patients. We used the negative logarithm of the estimated density as the uncertainty score, with higher values indicating greater unfamiliarity: with class frequencies 𝜋 𝑐 , means 𝜇 𝑐 and covariances 𝛴 𝑐 ; high values of 𝑠(ℎ) indicate a patient unlike the training data.

Five further variants were evaluated on the same representations: a covariance shared across classes, a three-component mixture per class, the density on lengthnormalized representations 53 , a background-corrected relative density score, and the relative Mahalanobis distance of Ren et al. 26 (Supplementary Note 7). The density was also refitted on a class-balanced subset of the training pool as a sensitivity analysis.

Evaluation

Discrimination was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and by the area under the precision-recall curve relative to the mortality rate (AUPRC lift). The primary calibration measure was the calibration slope, estimated by a logistic regression of each patient's observed outcome on the model's log-odds, without grouping patients into bins 6, 54 . A slope of 1 is ideal; below 1, high predicted risks are too high and low predicted risks too low. A linear fit on the deciles of Fig. 1 served as a sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Note 5).

We also report the expected calibration error over deciles of the predicted risk (ECE; Supplementary Note 6) 55, 56 and the cross-entropy relative to a constant prediction of the mortality rate (skill; Supplementary Fig. 7).

Each uncertainty measure was evaluated at three levels, corresponding to each of the research questions:

Level 1, cohort separation, is the AUROC of the measure for distinguishing external from internal test patients: the probability that a randomly chosen external patient has the higher value, with 0.5 corresponding to chance and values above 0.5 to a measure that rises after transfer.

Level 2, error detection, is the AUROC of the measure for distinguishing misclassified from correctly classified external patients. Errors were those of the prediction used together with the uncertainty measure: for single-model and Monte Carlo measures those of the model's own prediction without dropout, for ensemble measures those of the ensemble mean.

Level 3, selective prediction, asks whether deferring the most uncertain patients to clinical review reduces the errors among those who remain. Patients were accepted from the most certain downward, and the misclassification rate among the k accepted patients, 𝑅(𝑘), was averaged over all 𝑘 to give the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) 57, 58 . Subtracting the area of an oracle that accepts all correctly classified patients first removes the effect of the overall error rate 59 :

Lower values are better, and 0 is ideal. We also report the misclassification rate among the accepted patients when the 20% most uncertain are deferred (risk at 80% coverage). Patients with identical uncertainty measure values were accepted in the order of the cohort file, so that the result is reproducible (Supplementary Note 8).

Levels 2 and 3 were also computed on the internal test set as a baseline without distribution shift (Supplementary Table 12). Together, the three levels correspond to the two use cases examined in this study: Level 1 tests whether a measure warns of poorer overall performance after transfer, and Levels 2 and 3 whether it identifies the predictions that need review.

Table 4 summarizes what each measure quantifies and which question it addresses directly; here P(Y | X) denotes the probability of the outcome Y given a patient's inputs X, which the model estimates, and P(X) the distribution of the inputs themselves.

Data availability

The used databases, MIMIC-IV v3.1 and eICU-CRD v2.0, are available from PhysioNet (https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv/3.1/ and https://physionet.org/content/eicu-crd/2.0/) to credentialed users under a data use agreement. The derived cohorts cannot be shared under the agreement but can be regenerated from the raw data with the code below. The aggregated results underlying all figures and tables are provided in the Supplementary Information and in the code repository.

Use of large language models A large language model was used during manuscript preparation solely for language editing, proofreading, and for writing analysis code to the authors' specifications, which the authors reviewed. It was not used to generate scientific content, perform analyses, interpret results, or draft the manuscript independently. Ethics

This study is a secondary analysis of two publicly available, de-identified critical care databases. MIMIC-IV was approved by the institutional review boards of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and eICU-CRD was released under the HIPAA safe harbor provision after certification of its de-identification 37, 38 . Both are available under a data use agreement.

Fig 1 |

Fig 1 | Calibration before and after transfer. Observed mortality against predicted probability for the three architectures on the internal test set (top) and the external cohort (bottom): the logistic recalibration line, and a flexible spline curve with its range over seeds. Decile points show means over seeds with ±1 SD. Curves stop below 1.0 because almost no patients received higher predicted probabilities; decile points end lower because each decile contains one tenth of the patients.

Fig 2 |

Fig 2 | Mutual information and representation density.Top row: mutual information from Monte Carlo dropout, a measure of epistemic uncertainty, on a logarithmic x-axis. Bottom row: negative log-density, a measure of distance in the representation space of the last layer (higher values indicate greater distance from the centers of the training data). Blue: internal test set; red: external cohort. Dotted vertical lines: median of each cohort, with the ten seed models pooled. Boxes: cohort separation (AUROC, mean over the ten seed models).

Fig 3 |

Fig.3| Deferring patients per architecture. The y-axis gives the errors remaining among the accepted patients as a share of the full cohort. Lines are means over ten seeds, shaded bands the range. Excess areas of all measures are given in Supplementary Table6; the corresponding risk-coverage curves are shown in Supplementary Fig.6.

Fig 4 |

Fig 4 | Uncertainty measures across cohort separation, error detection, and selective prediction. Patient-level analyses use the external cohort. Higher AUROC and lower excess area under the risk-coverage curve (E-AURC) indicate better performance.Points show means across ten training seeds with 95% t-intervals; ensembles show full-ensemble estimates with leave-one-member-out ranges. Errors are those of the deterministic model or, for ensemble measures, the ensemble mean (classification threshold τ = 0.1288, the mortality rate of the training pool). Dashed lines mark chance (AUROC 0.5). The logit variance is plotted with reversed sign (-1 × logit variance): its AUROCs here equal 1 minus the values in the Results and Supplementary Table6, and its E-AURC corresponds to deferring the patients with the lowest logit variance first. MC, Monte Carlo.

Fig 5 |

Fig 5 | Deferral per 100 patients. Patients sorted by predictive entropy, H(p), into bins of ten (single-model entropy, means over the three architectures and ten seeds). Errors: share of all misclassifications falling in the bin. The 19 misclassified patients per 100 are the mean misclassification rate of the three architectures (GRU 17.5%, LSTM 18.9%, transformer 20.1%).
